title: First and last position of an element
prompt:
A sorted list holds the reading levels of a class's assigned books. When the teacher filters by one level, the app needs the range of books at that level.

Write firstAndLast(nums, target) that returns [firstIndex, lastIndex] of target in the sorted array nums, or [-1, -1] if it isn't there. Must run in O(log n) time, even if every element equals the target. Values may be decimals, so don't rely on target + 1.

Examples with nums = [5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10]:

  • firstAndLast(nums, 8) → [3, 4]
  • firstAndLast(nums, 6) → [-1, -1]
  • firstAndLast([], 0) → [-1, -1]

Constraints: 0 ≤ nums.length ≤ 105, sorted in non-decreasing order.

tests.name: matches a linear scan on many small inputs

hints: Finding one copy and walking outward is O(n) when there are many copies. Instead, ask two different yes/no questions that each flip once, and binary search each.
First = the first index where nums[i] >= target. If that index is past the end or doesn't hold the target, return [-1, -1]. Last = (the first index where nums[i] > target) − 1.

Write the template once and pass the question in:

function firstIndexWhere(nums, isYes) {
  let lo = 0, hi = nums.length;
  while (lo < hi) {
    const mid = lo + Math.floor((hi - lo) / 2);
    if (isYes(nums[mid])) hi = mid;
    else lo = mid + 1;
  }
  return lo;
}
// first = firstIndexWhere(nums, v => v >= target)
// last  = firstIndexWhere(nums, v => v > target) - 1
explain:
Time O(log n), space O(1). Two binary searches, about 2 × log₂ n checks, even if a million elements equal the target. The count of matches is simply last - first + 1, which is how you answer "how many books are at level 3?" in O(log n).

In an interview: "I'll run the same lower-bound binary search twice: the first index with value at least the target, and the first index with value greater than the target. The range between them is the answer. Both are O(log n), and walking outward would be O(n) with many duplicates."
